intro: Today you'll learn to say who things belong to, like Rina's phone, and to ask Whose …? when you don't know the owner. You'll also meet me, him, her, us and them, the words for people that come after an action word (a verb) like call or help. Warm-up: think of one thing on your table and who it belongs to.
teachingNotes: Indonesian puts the owner AFTER the thing (HP Rina, mobil ayah saya); English puts owner + 's FIRST: Rina's phone, my father's car. Typical errors: *phone Rina, *Rina phone, *the phone of Rina.

Object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) go after a verb (I love her) or after a small word like with, for, to (Come with us). Indonesian 'dia' and '-nya' cover he/him/she/her, so learners say *She loves he or *I know she. Contrast subject vs object: he → him, she → her, we → us, they → them.
Don't add 'to' after call, help, meet, visit, love or know: Call me later, not *Call to me later (from Indonesian 'telepon ke saya').

Whose asks about the owner: Whose + thing + is this? (Whose pen is this?). Answer with 's: It's Andi's. / It's Andi's pen. Whose and who's sound the same; who's = who is. Also note that 's can mean 'is' (Rina's a nurse) — context tells.

Explain the jargon in plain words: subject = the one who does the action (before the verb); object = the one who receives it (after the verb); verb = action word. Point out that 'her' has two jobs (her bag = tasnya; I call her = meneleponnya), that English needs it/them where Indonesian drops the object (Saya suka = I like it), and that the -s in loves/works/teaches comes from the simple present (not a prerequisite here): just say 'with one person the verb gets -s, you'll learn it later'. In 'It's Andi's', the first 's = is and the second 's = belongs to. English 'brother/sister' covers both kakak and adik.

Limits: don't teach possessive pronouns (mine, yours, hers) or plural s' (my parents' house) yet — accept them if the learner uses them correctly. Use 'this' in Whose questions (these/those come in a later lesson). No past or future forms; simple present and be only. Avoid owner names ending in -s (Agus, Dimas); if one comes up, accept both Agus's and Agus'.

keyPoints.title: Possessive 's
keyPoints.explanation: Owner + 's + thing. The owner comes FIRST in English: Rina's phone (HP Rina), my mother's name (nama ibu saya). The small mark ' (apostrophe) + s means 'belongs to'; an s without it means 'more than one' (cars).

keyPoints.title: Object pronouns
keyPoints.explanation: The one who does the action (the subject) comes before the verb: I, he, she, we, they. The one who receives it (the object) comes after a verb or after with/for/to: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. No 'to' after call, help or know: these verbs take the person directly.

keyPoints.title: Whose …?
keyPoints.explanation: Ask about the owner with Whose + thing + is this? Answer with 's: It's Andi's (pen). In 'It's Andi's' the first 's = is, the second 's = belongs to Andi.

examples.en: Whose pen is this? — It's Andi's.
Whose glass is this? — It's my glass.

blocks.text: To say who owns something, put the **owner first**, add **'s**, then the thing: **Rina's phone**. Indonesian does it the other way round (*HP Rina*), so don't translate word by word. The small mark **'** is called an *apostrophe*. **'s** with it means 'belongs to' (*Rina's* = milik Rina). An **s** without it means 'more than one' (*two cars*).

id.text: Untuk menyebut pemilik sesuatu, letakkan **pemiliknya dulu**, tambahkan **'s**, lalu bendanya: **Rina's phone**. Bahasa Indonesia urutannya terbalik (*HP Rina*), jadi jangan menerjemahkan kata per kata. Tanda kecil **'** namanya *apostrof*. **'s** dengan tanda itu artinya 'milik' (*Rina's* = milik Rina). Huruf **s** tanpa tanda itu artinya 'lebih dari satu' (*two cars*).

rows.en: The teacher's desk is near the door.
rows.id: Meja guru ada di dekat pintu.

blocks.text: Not *phone Rina* and not *Rina phone*: always **Rina's phone**. And careful: **'s** can also mean **is**. *Rina's a nurse* = Rina is a nurse. How to tell: if a thing comes right after (*Rina's phone*), 's = belongs to. If *a/an* or a describing word comes after (*Rina's a nurse, Rina's tired*), 's = is.

id.text: Bukan *phone Rina* dan bukan *Rina phone*: selalu **Rina's phone**. Hati-hati juga: **'s** bisa berarti **is**. *Rina's a nurse* = Rina is a nurse. Cara membedakannya: kalau langsung diikuti benda (*Rina's phone*), 's = milik. Kalau diikuti *a/an* atau kata sifat (*Rina's a nurse, Rina's tired*), 's = is.

blocks.explain: Owner first (my sister) + 's + thing (room): my sister's room.

id.explain: Pemilik dulu (my sister) + 's + benda (room): my sister's room.

blocks.text: The person who **does** the action (the *subject*) comes before the verb: **I, he, she, we, they**. The person who **receives** the action (the *object*) comes **after** a verb, or after small words like **with, for, to**: **me, you, him, her, it, us, them**. Indonesian uses *dia* or *-nya* for both, but English changes the word: ***She** loves **him**.* (A *verb* is an action word: love, call, help.)

id.text: Orang yang **melakukan** kegiatan (*subjek*) ada sebelum kata kerja: **I, he, she, we, they**. Orang yang **dikenai** kegiatan (*objek*) ada **setelah** kata kerja, atau setelah kata kecil seperti **with, for, to**: **me, you, him, her, it, us, them**. Bahasa Indonesia memakai *dia* atau *-nya* untuk keduanya, tapi bahasa Inggris mengganti katanya: ***She** loves **him**.* (*Kata kerja* = kata kegiatan: love, call, help.)

rows.en: Rina is my best friend. I call her every day.
rows.id: Rina sahabat saya. Saya meneleponnya setiap hari.
Pak Hadi mengajari kami bahasa Inggris. (*teaches*: satu orang → kata kerjanya diberi -es)

rows.en: This coffee is good. I like it.
rows.id: Kopi ini enak. Saya suka. (bahasa Inggris tetap butuh *it*)

rows.en: My shoes are old. I don't like them.
rows.id: Sepatu saya sudah tua. Saya tidak suka. (bahasa Inggris tetap butuh *them*)

blocks.text: No **to** after call, help, meet or visit: **Call me later**, not *Call to me later*. Indonesian can say *telepon ke saya*, but in English these verbs take the person directly, with nothing in between.

id.text: Tidak ada **to** setelah call, help, meet atau visit: **Call me later**, bukan *Call to me later*. Bahasa Indonesia bisa bilang *telepon ke saya*, tapi dalam bahasa Inggris kata kerja ini langsung diikuti orangnya, tanpa kata di tengah.

blocks.text:
Three things that surprise beginners:
- **English needs the object.** *Saya suka* is fine in Indonesian, but English says **I like it** / **I like them**.
- **her has two jobs:** *her bag* (tasnya, milik dia) and *I call her* (meneleponnya). For a man they are different words: *his bag*, *I call him*.
- **loves, works, teaches:** with one person (he, she, Budi) the verb gets **-s**. You'll learn why in the Simple Present lesson; for now, just notice it.

id.text:
Tiga hal yang sering bikin bingung:
- **Bahasa Inggris butuh objeknya.** *Saya suka* sudah cukup dalam bahasa Indonesia, tapi bahasa Inggris bilang **I like it** / **I like them**.
- **her punya dua tugas:** *her bag* (tasnya, milik dia) dan *I call her* (meneleponnya). Untuk laki-laki katanya beda: *his bag*, *I call him*.
- **loves, works, teaches:** dengan satu orang (he, she, Budi) kata kerjanya diberi **-s**. Alasannya kamu pelajari di pelajaran Simple Present; sekarang cukup perhatikan saja.

blocks.prompt: Mr. Hadi is our teacher. We like ___ very much.
blocks.explain: The word comes after the verb like, so we need the 'after the verb' form (object pronoun): he → him. his means 'belongs to him' (his bag).

id.explain: Katanya ada setelah kata kerja like, jadi kita butuh bentuk 'setelah kata kerja' (object pronoun): he → him. his artinya 'milik dia' (his bag).

blocks.text: When you don't know the owner, ask **Whose + thing + is this?** *Whose pen is this?* Answer with 's: **It's Andi's.** or **It's Andi's pen.** You can also answer with my, your, his or her: *It's my pen.*

id.text: Kalau kamu tidak tahu pemiliknya, tanyakan **Whose + benda + is this?** *Whose pen is this?* Jawab dengan 's: **It's Andi's.** atau **It's Andi's pen.** Kamu juga bisa menjawab dengan my, your, his atau her: *It's my pen.*

rows.en: Whose pen is this? — It's Andi's.
Whose glass is this? — It's my glass.
rows.id: Gelas siapa ini? — Itu gelas saya.

rows.en: Whose motorbike is this? — It's Pak Joko's.
rows.id: Motor siapa ini? — Punya Pak Joko.

blocks.text: **Whose** and **who's** sound the same, but **who's** = **who is**: *Who's your teacher?* For the owner, write **whose**. And in the answer **It's Andi's**, the two 's do different jobs: **It's** = It **is**, **Andi's** = milik Andi. We can stop after *Andi's* because we already know the thing (the pen).

id.text: **Whose** dan **who's** bunyinya sama, tapi **who's** = **who is**: *Who's your teacher?* Untuk menanyakan pemilik, tulis **whose**. Lalu dalam jawaban **It's Andi's**, dua 's itu tugasnya beda: **It's** = It **is**, **Andi's** = milik Andi. Kita boleh berhenti di *Andi's* karena bendanya (pulpen) sudah jelas.

blocks.explain: We ask about the owner, so whose. Who's means who is.

id.explain: Kita menanyakan pemiliknya, jadi whose. Who's artinya who is.

blocks.text: You'll use these words every day. At the office: *Whose cup is this? — It's Bu Ani's.* On the phone: *Please call me after lunch.* At school: *Our teacher helps us a lot. We like her.*

id.text: Kamu akan memakai kata-kata ini setiap hari. Di kantor: *Whose cup is this? — It's Bu Ani's.* Di telepon: *Please call me after lunch.* Di sekolah: *Our teacher helps us a lot. We like her.*
